[PAPER_0061, relevance_score=0.471] Method

Transparency and Openness

The present article is based on data from the five-wave longitudinal Post-Event Changes Study. Data collection for this study was approved by local ethics committee of Ruhr-University Bochum (Protocol No. 702). The design of the Post-Event Changes Study was preregistered at https://osf.io/hm3rv/?view_only=21bd4c93496345f783f63f43b369481c.

[PAPER_0064, relevance_score=0.407] Procedure

The Post-Event Changes Study was conducted online in 2021 and 2022 in Germany. The study was addressed to people who had recently experienced a negative major life event. At the initial registration, people interested in participating in the Post-Event Changes Study provided informed consent, verified their age (minimum age: 18 years), and confirmed that they had experienced one of five negative major life events in the last 5 weeks (death of a loved one, separation, job loss, friendship dissolution, or failing an important exam).

[PAPER_0067, relevance_score=0.417] Participants

Only people who experienced one of the following five major life events in the last 5 weeks were eligible for inclusion in the study: death of a loved one, separation, friendship dissolution, job loss, or failing an important exam. We chose this study design of recruiting participants after they experienced a certain life event to be able to target recruitment on those people (e.g., by posting in event-related online forums). This strategy allowed us to achieve larger sample sizes for specific life events compared to a sampling strategy addressed to the general public.

[PAPER_0068, relevance_score=0.360] As compensation for participation and to reduce dropout, there were voucher raffles with increasing value after each measurement occasion. Furthermore, psychology students were able to receive partial course credit for their participation.

In total, 1,673 people registered to take part in the Post-Event Changes Study. As the event characteristics were assessed at T1, only participants who took part at T1 could be included in the analyses.

[PAPER_0073, relevance_score=0.352] Supplemental Section 2 ).

Based on the sample sizes and dropout rate in the present study, we conducted several power simulations using the R package simr (Green & MacLeod, 2016). These power simulations showed that our analyses for the events of separation, death of a loved one, and friendship dissolution were sufficiently powered to detect medium-sized effects (differences of d = 0.41 over 6 months, as, for example, found in a study on perceived event characteristics by Luhmann et al., 2021).

[PAPER_0093, relevance_score=0.400] Associations Among Event Characteristics

To address Research Question 1 (association between perceived event characteristics and objective-descriptive event characteristics), we computed measures of associations depending on the scale type of the objective-descriptive event characteristics. For metric and dichotomous objective-descriptive event characteristics, we calculated correlation coefficients. For polytomous objective-descriptive event characteristics, we computed one-way analyses of variance with the perceived event characteristics as dependent variables and used η2 as effect size measure.

[PAPER_0094, relevance_score=0.356] Furthermore, for each major life event, we computed multiple regressions using the perceived event characteristics as dependent variables and all objective-descriptive event characteristics as predictors to estimate how much variance of the perceived event characteristics could be explained by all objective-descriptive event characteristics together.

[PAPER_0095, relevance_score=0.422] Examining Changes in SWB Using Specification Curve Analyses

To answer Research Questions 2-4, we used longitudinal multilevel models with measurement occasions (Level 1) nested in participants (Level 2). As there were many reasonable ways to specify these multilevel models, and as we assumed that certain analytical choices might influence the results of interest, we combined these multilevel models with specification curve analysis (Simonsohn et al., 2020).

[PAPER_0116, relevance_score=0.431] Step 3: Joint Statistical Test

After creating this descriptive specification curve, joint statistical tests can be computed for the different extracted effects. In our case, we tested the statistical significance of the main effect of an event characteristic (i.e., whether an event characteristic is associated with individual differences at the timepoint of the event occurrence) and the cross-level interaction with time (i.e., whether an event characteristic is associated with individual differences in changes in SWB).

[PAPER_0122, relevance_score=0.422] As these three joint statistical tests were used to address the same question (whether the full set of specifications speaks against the null hypothesis that there is no effect), we used a Bonferroni-corrected level of significance of α = .05/3 = .0167 for these tests.

We will use indicator variable method and full information maximum likelihood for model estimation. [PREREG_0028, relevance_score=0.496] q17.question: To address Research Question 1 (association between perceived and objective-descriptive event characteristics), we will compute correlation coefficients (for metric and dichotomous objective-descriptive event characteristics) and one-way ANOVAs (for polytomous objective-descriptive event characteristics).

To address Research Question 2 (predicting event-related changes in subjective well-being using objective-descriptive and perceived event characteristics), we will use longitudinal multilevel models with measurement occasions (Level 1) nested in participants (Level 2).

[PREREG_0030, relevance_score=0.416] Regarding the model specifications of these multilevel models, there are several valid possibilities (e.g., regarding the coding of time or the inclusion of covariates). We will therefore combine the longitudinal multilevel models with specification curve analysis (Simonsohn et al., 2020). Specification curve analysis is a possible way to deal with cases in which there are many possible, valid ways to analyze the data. The idea behind specification curve analysis is that all possible specifications are computed and then the robustness of the effects is tested among different specifications.

[PREREG_0037, relevance_score=0.426] q19: We will use a level of significance of α = .05 for our analyses of Research Question 1 and in Step 2 of specification curve analysis (i.e., the evaluation of the statistical significance of fixed effects and model comparisons). However, in Step 3 of the specification curve analysis, three statistical tests are computed that are used to evaluate the same question. Therefore, we will use Bonferroni-corrected level of significance of α = .05/3 = .0167 for this step (for a similar procedure see Beck & Jackson, 2022).

[PAPER_0104, relevance_score=0.348] We either used a linear time variable (timelin) or a logarithmic time variable (timelog) in our analyses.2 The linear time variable described the temporal distance between the event occurrence and each measurement occasion in months. For example, if a participant took part in T1 half a month after the event occurrence, the linear time variable would be coded as follows: 0.5 at T1, 1.5 at T2, 2.5 at T3, 4.5 at T4, and 6.5 at T5.

[PAPER_0105, relevance_score=0.323] To create a logarithmic time variable, we transformed the linear time in the following way: timelog = log(1 + timelin). This logarithmic time variable captures nonlinear changes in SWB with pronounced changes shortly after the event occurrence and less change with increasing temporal distance to the event occurrence (e.g., Luhmann et al., 2012). For both time codings, time = 0 is the timepoint of the event occurrence.

[PAPER_0106, relevance_score=0.243] However, it should be noted that this intercept (i.e., the SWB at the timepoint of the event occurrence) is an extrapolation for most participants, as participants joined the study shortly after the occurrence of the negative event.

Furthermore, we recoded several of our variables to ease interpretation of the corresponding coefficients. First, we recoded negative affect such that higher values represent less negative affect, so that for all three SWB components, higher values indicate a higher SWB.

[PAPER_0107, relevance_score=0.349] Second, all metric variables were standardized using their grand mean and standard deviation so that the corresponding fixed effects can be interpreted in standard deviation units. Third, for all dichotomous predictors, we used dummy coding. Consequently, fixed effects indicate the mean-level differences between the two categories. For all polytomous predictors, we applied weighted deviation coding using the contr.wec-function of the R package wec (Nieuwenhuis et al., 2017).
